clue.text: Celebs inching extremely close to John Virgo, say

parts.note: celebrities are stars

indicators.note: taking a word extremely means keeping only its two outermost letters
the close of the name John is its final letter

explanation.surface: Famous people edging nearer to the snooker player and commentator John Virgo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John Virgo' reads as one name, but John only supplies its last letter and Virgo, with 'say', is the definition. 'extremely' gives the ends of inching.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, so it is an example of an astrological sign.

clue.text: Neighbours, as one, going on strike for campaign platform

indicators.note: going on means following after, so this piece comes second

parts.note: Neighbours is an Australian television soap opera
to box is to hit or strike

explanation.surface: People next door, united in going on strike for an election platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neighbours, as one' looks like people acting together but means the TV soap.
explanation.definitionFit: A soapbox is an improvised stand from which a speaker addresses the public, a platform for campaigning.

clue.text: Conjecture sport will return after one month

indicators.note: after places this piece behind the month

parts.note: Aug is the abbreviation for August

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: Guessing that a sport will come back after a month off.
explanation.definitionFit: To augur is to predict or foretell, which is to conjecture about the future.

clue.text: Take a cocktail, having time out for a chat maybe

indicators.note: out here means removed, so the time letter is taken away from the cocktail

parts.note: a stinger is a cocktail of brandy and crème de menthe

explanation.surface: Someone drinking a cocktail during a break for a gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chat' is not talk but the songbird; 'Take' and 'having' are only links. 'out' removes T from STINGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat is a small songbird such as the stonechat, so it is an example of a singer.

clue.text: Cut good wood

parts.note: ash is a timber, the wood of the ash tree

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut decent timber.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a deep slash or wound, a cut.

clue.text: Unctuous host pursuing controlling sex

indicators.note: the host follows behind, so it is placed after the other piece

parts.note: SM, short for sadomasochism, is sex built on domination and control
a host is a great multitude, especially an army

explanation.surface: A greasy party host chasing after kinky domination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'host' looks like the party giver but is the old sense of an army.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone ingratiating with oily, excessive charm.

clue.text: Spotted poor soul being restrained by staff

indicators.note: restrained by means held inside the other piece

parts.note: a mace is a ceremonial staff

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wretched person seen being held back by employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees but is a rod; 'poor' rearranges SOUL to ULOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Maculose is a technical word for covered in spots or blotches, from the Latin for spot.

clue.text: When could it be this uncouth?

parts.note: read as wordplay, the answer says to make the letters of hewn rough, a rearrangement that gives when

explanation.surface: Asking at what point something becomes crude.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'rough' is the anagram signal in the answer, and the shuffled HEWN makes WHEN, the clue's first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-hewn means crudely shaped, and of a person unrefined or uncultured.

clue.text: Husband may ask to alter veil

indicators.note: to alter is to change, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A husband might request that a veil be changed.
explanation.definitionFit: A yashmak is the veil worn by some Muslim women to cover the face in public.

clue.text: Parasites found in stream POW churned up

indicators.note: churned up means stirred violently, so these letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: Bugs discovered in a river that a prisoner of war stirred up.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapeworms are flat parasitic worms living in the intestines of their hosts.

clue.text: Gas from uncontained fart expanded to the max?

indicators.note: losing what contains it means the outer letters of the phrase are dropped, leaving its core

parts.note: far gone means taken to an extreme, and it is also the word fart with its last letter stretched out

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke about wind let loose and swelling as far as it can go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncontained' strips F and E from the ends of FAR GONE. A second layer: fart without its ends is AR, the chemical symbol, and 'expanded' writes it out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, a colourless inert gas found in air.

clue.text: Use coasts to manoeuvre? We might

definitions.text: Use coasts to manoeuvre? We might

indicators.note: to manoeuvre is to shift things around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Young sailors volunteering that they might steer along the shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We might' makes the whole clue the speaker's own boast: the young people who would work the coasts are themselves the anagram of USE COASTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea scouts are a branch of the Scout movement trained in boating and seamanship, so handling coastal waters is their activity.

clue.text: Row by inlet secreting navy base

indicators.note: secreting means hiding something away inside

parts.note: a bay is an inlet of the sea
RN is the Royal Navy
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: An argument beside a creek where a naval base is tucked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is only a link; 'base' is the mathematical e, not a military base.
explanation.definitionFit: A barney is British slang for a noisy quarrel, the same as a row.

clue.text: Dog leash may hurt

indicators.note: something hurt is damaged or knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that the lead could injure the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sealyham is a small Welsh terrier breed, so it is one kind of dog.

clue.text: Take a deep breath and oppress play despite not knowing the score

definitions.text: play despite not knowing the score

parts.note: to sigh is to breathe out deeply
to tread down is to oppress

explanation.surface: Breathing deeply and crushing a stage play while ignorant of the result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' looks like the result of a game but is printed music.
explanation.definitionFit: To sight-read is to perform music on first seeing it, without having learnt the score.

clue.text: Uncle abroad cross about annual holiday

indicators.note: turned about means read in the opposite direction

parts.note: Uncle Sam personifies the United States, seen from abroad
X is a cross shape

explanation.surface: An uncle overseas is grumpy about the yearly break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like angry but is the letter X; 'about' turns round both pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Xmas is the common short written form of Christmas, a festival held every year.

clue.text: Challenging circuit is to lap old university

parts.note: an ambit is a circuit or compass

indicators.note: to lap is to wrap round, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: OU is the Open University

explanation.surface: A demanding race track has to circle an ancient college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old' is not a hint of age here; OU is the Open University.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambitious plan or task is one that is demanding, challenging to carry out.

clue.text: Arguably highbrow point in unnoted opening talk

indicators.note: un-noted means with the note taken away; N is the dictionary abbreviation for note

parts.note: a window is an opening in a wall
to talk is to speak

explanation.surface: A lofty argument made in an unscripted opening speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unnoted' drops N (note) from WINDOW. 'highbrow' is used literally: the point of hair high on the brow.
explanation.definitionFit: A widow's peak is a V-shaped point of hairline in the middle of the forehead, literally a point high on the brow.

clue.text: Priest perhaps secure in St. James's area

parts.note: a priest is a small club used by anglers to kill fish
to land is to secure or win something

explanation.surface: A clergyman perhaps finding a place in a parish of St James.
explanation.walkthrough: St James's is a district of central London full of gentlemen's clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubland is the name for the St James's district of London, home of exclusive gentlemen's clubs.

clue.text: Gang deployed Emile to pinch house trailer

parts.note: a mob is a gang

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip, holding the other piece inside
deployed means spread out and arranged differently, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A gang sends Emile off to steal a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinch' looks like steal but means grip: the shuffled Emile holds the house abbreviation inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobile home is a large caravan or trailer that people live in.

clue.text: Shares with awfully sick miners, backing shelters

indicators.note: shelters means encloses, so one piece goes inside
backing means moving in reverse, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Stock owned by ill miners propping up refuges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shares' looks like stock but is the verb. The NUM is the British miners' union.
explanation.definitionFit: To muck in is to share work or lodgings with others, so it is an idiom for sharing.

clue.text: Equipment cut by northern contract

indicators.note: being cut by something means it is split with that piece inserted

parts.note: kit is equipment

explanation.surface: Gear slashed by a northern firm's deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contract' looks like a noun but is the verb, as in knitting one's brows.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to draw together or tighten, as brows knit in a frown, so it means contract.

clue.text: Ancient citizens in bar finish off these when getting round

indicators.note: getting round something means surrounding it
finishing off means cutting away the word's end

parts.note: to ban is to bar

explanation.surface: Old regulars in a pub finishing off their drinks as their round comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish off' takes the last letter from these, leaving THES, which goes round BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Thebans were citizens of Thebes, a city of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Source of fizz in cellar originally acquired by fluke

indicators.note: acquired by means taken into the other piece

parts.note: a fluke is the barbed head of a harpoon or arrow, so a barb

indicators.note: originally points to the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A bubbly wine kept in the cellar came there by sheer luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fluke' looks like luck but is the barbed head of a harpoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Bicarb, bicarbonate of soda, releases carbon dioxide and makes things fizz.

clue.text: Concise when penning article about British conchie

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the other piece goes inside

parts.note: curt means short or concise

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the article is wrapped round the letter for British

parts.note: the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A short note about Britain written by a pacifist.
explanation.walkthrough: A conchie is a conscientious objector; Cuthbert was the WWI nickname for men who dodged call-up, a near enough match.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuthbert was First World War slang for a man accused of dodging military service, close to a conscientious objector.

clue.text: Creator of said Holy Land?

parts.note: a gardening tool that pokes holes in soil makes holey land, a phrase that sounds like Holy Land

explanation.surface: Asking who made the biblical Holy Land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' points out that Holy should be heard as holey: ground full of holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A dibble is a pointed hand tool for making holes in the ground for seeds and bulbs.

clue.text: Chap with no money having switched sides

indicators.note: switching sides swaps right for left, R for L

parts.note: broke means penniless

explanation.surface: A penniless man who has defected.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloke is informal British for a man, a chap.

clue.text: Addict given bum steer off and on

indicators.note: off and on means skipping one letter then taking the next, picking every other letter

explanation.surface: A drug user misled with bad advice now and again.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is someone who takes illegal drugs, an addict.

clue.text: They travel gratis to arrange half of league fixtures

parts.note: to stow is to pack or arrange things
in a league each team plays half its games away, and those matches are called aways

explanation.surface: A list of football league fixtures being sorted out, with free travel thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: In British football a team's season is half home games and half aways.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowaways hide on ships or planes to make the journey without paying a fare.

clue.text: Bouquet inamorata holds back

indicators.note: held back means the letters run backwards
the word inamorata holds the answer's letters within it

explanation.surface: A lover clutching flowers behind her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' hides AMORA inside inamorata, and 'back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine's bouquet is its smell, its aroma.

clue.text: Patent legend in US returned for end of rugby match

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Thomas Edison, the American inventor, held over a thousand patents

explanation.surface: An American inventor whose patent comes back to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patent legend' looks like an inscription but means a legendary patent holder.
explanation.definitionFit: No side is the referee's call ending a rugby match.

clue.text: These stir soil, ultimately making uneven places

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of making

parts.note: in bowls a rub or rubber is an uneven patch of the green that deflects a bowl

explanation.surface: Things that churn the earth and end up leaving lumpy ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uneven places' comes from the game of lawn bowls, where an irregularity of the green is a rub or rubber.
explanation.definitionFit: Grubbers are tools or implements for digging up roots and breaking up soil.
